content: Bronchiolitis is the most common lower respiratory tract infection in pediatric patients aged between 1 month and 2 years. It is primarily caused by the respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) and is characterized by inflammation, edema, and necrosis of the bronchiolar epithelium. Histologically, bronchiolitis can be classified into bronchiolitis obliterans, proliferative bronchiolitis, diffuse panbronchiolitis, or respiratory bronchiolitis. The Bronchiolitis Severity Score (BSS) is used to categorize the disease into four classes. Typical clinical manifestations include rhinorrhea, cough, wheezing, respiratory crackles, use of accessory respiratory muscles, and nasal flaring. In adults, risk factors for developing bronchiolitis include exposure to cigarette smoke, living in crowded environments, and being immunocompromised. In infants, risk factors include age under 6 months, lack of breastfeeding, prematurity, and congenital heart diseases. The cornerstone of treatment is supportive therapy. Bronchiolitis was first reported in 1899 by researchers at the University of Minnesota and was fully described in 1901 by Dr. Lange. Classification of bronchiolitis is based on the patient’s age and histological features. It is categorized as either adult or infant bronchiolitis based on age. Histologically, it can be classified as acute infectious bronchiolitis, bronchiolitis obliterans, proliferative bronchiolitis, diffuse panbronchiolitis, or respiratory bronchiolitis. The BSS further divides the disease into four severity classes. Bronchiolitis is transmitted via airborne droplets. RSV infects the nasopharyngeal mucosa and spreads to the lower airways, where viral replication occurs in the bronchioles. This leads to inflammation, edema, and necrosis of the bronchiolar epithelium. The exposure of subepithelial tissue and nerve fibers triggers the cough reflex. Increased vascular permeability results in edema and swelling. Histopathologically, bronchiolitis obliterans is characterized by intraluminal polyps, inflammatory infiltration, and macrophages, while constrictive bronchiolitis shows airway thickening and luminal narrowing. Bronchiolitis predominantly affects children under 2 years of age, with a peak incidence between 3 and 6 months. RSV is the most common cause, but other viruses such as adenovirus, influenza, and parainfluenza can also be responsible. Bacterial organisms like Legionella pneumophila and Mycoplasma pneumoniae may also cause bronchiolitis. Noninfectious causes include smoking, collagen vascular diseases, and post-bone marrow transplant conditions. Bronchiolitis must be differentiated from other respiratory and cardiac diseases with similar clinical presentations, such as asthma, COPD, pneumonia, congestive heart failure, diffuse idiopathic neuroendocrine cell hyperplasia, tuberculosis, pertussis, foreign body aspiration, pulmonary embolism, and Harman-Rich syndrome. Bronchiolitis is one of the most common acute respiratory diseases in infants and children, affecting approximately 3,000 per 100,000 children in the United States. It occurs predominantly during the fall, winter, and early spring. While it can affect any age group, it is most common in infants under 2 years, particularly boys, and is more prevalent among Native Americans, Alaskans, and Hispanics. Despite high hospitalization rates, the mortality rate is low. Risk factors for bronchiolitis vary by age. In adults, common risk factors include exposure to cigarette smoke, crowded living conditions, and immunosuppression. In infants, risk factors include age under 6 months, lack of breastfeeding, prematurity, and congenital heart diseases. If untreated, bronchiolitis typically begins with mild upper respiratory symptoms, shortness of breath, wheezing, persistent cough, and tachypnea within the first 2–3 days. Chest wall retractions and nasal flaring often develop between days 3 and 7. Symptoms usually resolve within 2 weeks. Complications are more common in infants younger than 2 months, premature infants, and those with underlying medical conditions such as congenital heart disease, chronic pulmonary disease, or immunodeficiencies. Severity scores can help estimate prognosis. Common symptoms of bronchiolitis include fever, cough, dyspnea, and nasal discharge. Other symptoms may include post-tussive vomiting and dehydration. On physical examination, patients may appear toxic and cyanotic. Fever may or may not be present. Lung examination often reveals intercostal and substernal retractions on inspection, and wheezing and crackles with decreased respiratory sounds on auscultation. Extrapulmonary manifestations such as pharyngitis, conjunctivitis, arrhythmias, tachycardia, and seizures may also occur. Diagnosis of bronchiolitis is primarily clinical, based on symptoms and physical examination. Laboratory tests are not specific for the disease. Commonly used tests include viral pathogen detection methods such as ELISA, immunofluorescent assays, and optical immunoassays. Complete blood count is nonspecific, and pulmonary function tests may help support the diagnosis and exclude other obstructive lung diseases. Chest X-rays in bronchiolitis are usually nonspecific and may show atelectasis and consolidations. They are primarily used to exclude other conditions such as pneumonia. CT scans may reveal centrilobular nodules, bronchiolar wall thickening, ground-glass opacities, and parenchymal cysts, but these findings are nonspecific. MRI and other imaging modalities do not provide additional diagnostic value. The primary treatment for bronchiolitis is supportive care, which includes frequent small feedings and oxygen therapy. In severe cases, intravenous fluids and nasogastric feeding may be required. Mechanical ventilation or continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) may be necessary in extreme cases. Prophylaxis is recommended for infants with hemodynamically significant heart disease and preterm infants requiring more than 21% oxygen for at least the first 28 days of life. Palivizumab is the drug of choice for prophylaxis. Surgical intervention is not recommended for bronchiolitis. Primary prevention measures include handwashing, avoiding contact with symptomatic individuals, and preventing tobacco smoke exposure. These measures aim to reduce viral transmission during the RSV season. Passive immunization with palivizumab is recommended for high-risk patients. There are no secondary preventive measures available for bronchiolitis.
